first.rationale:
The competitor's entry pricing creates pressure toward promotional_pricing, but memory_73 carries an explicit, unusually specific caveat: it lifted acquisition while materially reducing 30-day retention, with an instruction not to generalize it. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, matching price would buy volume that erodes at 30 days — the wrong trade, and the caveat is exactly the part of inherited memory most likely to be discarded under competitive urgency. I am declining that path deliberately, not by omission.

Of the remaining directions, two internal metrics are actually degrading: onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%). These are plausibly one causal chain rather than two problems — memory_86 links shortened onboarding to downstream adoption, so a completion decline would be expected to surface as an activation decline a step later. Treating onboarding as the upstream cause targets the root; activation_messaging would treat the symptom and is my fallback if verification undercuts the onboarding evidence.

I am spending both verification pulls on memory_31 and memory_86 because they are the load-bearing basis for my chosen action and they may not be independent. Both point the same direction, which makes them feel mutually confirming, but they could be two consolidations of one underlying experiment — in which case my evidence base is half as strong as it looks. I also want the original records to check scope: memory_31 is scoped to SMB activation and is the oldest item here (day 12, ~64 days stale), and memory_86 is scoped to self-serve accounts. If either lift was measured only in a segment or under conditions that no longer hold, the inference to today is weaker than the summary implies.

Downstream value risk: the specific mechanism in memory_31 is cutting required signup fields. Those fields plausibly feed lead qualification and routing. Per memory_44, enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted flows, so stripping fields indiscriminately could degrade demo-request routing and trade qualified pipeline for raw signup volume — a gain on the proxy metric that damages the actual objective. The experiment must be scoped to the self-serve/SMB path, preserve enterprise routing signals, and be read on activation and qualified-pipeline quality, not signup count alone.

Standard experiment scale with a retention and pipeline-quality guardrail; the evidence supports a real test but not a broad rollout, and the inherited lifts are summaries whose original conditions I have not yet confirmed.

final.rationale:
Verification changed the shape of this decision, and the change matters more than the conclusion. Both pulled summaries had lost material caveats in consolidation. memory_86 read as an unqualified win; the source shows +9% 60-day churn concentrated in complex-workspace accounts, because the shortened flow strips setup steps those accounts need, with an explicit instruction not to roll it out there. memory_31 survived intact but is narrower than it sounded: confirmed on SMB, explicitly not replicated on other segments. Two for two on caveat loss is itself a finding — I should treat the remaining unverified summaries (memory_57, memory_91, memory_44) as similarly likely to be missing conditions, and not lean on them as if they were clean.

Critically, these were never one intervention. exp_31 is signup field reduction; exp_86 is shortening the onboarding flow itself. My prior worry that they were redundant consolidations of one experiment was wrong in the opposite direction — they are distinct levers with distinct risk profiles, and bundling them would have quietly imported exp_86's churn mechanism into an otherwise safe test.

So I run only the exp_31 lever: reduce required signup fields, scoped to SMB self-serve accounts. That is the one direction with a confirmed record on the target objective rather than a proxy — +4% qualified revenue, activation +9%, retention -1%, which is the sustainable-revenue metric I am actually accountable to. I am not shortening the onboarding flow. Complex-workspace accounts are excluded by construction, not by hope.

I hold the decision against promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing. memory_73's caveat is the same species of caveat that consolidation just proved it strips: acquisition lift purchased with material 30-day retention loss. Competitive urgency is precisely the pressure that would make me discount it, so I discount it not at all.

Downstream value risk stands and is now sharper. Signup fields plausibly feed lead qualification and enterprise demo routing (memory_44). Cutting them indiscriminately would inflate raw signups while degrading qualified pipeline — a proxy win that damages the objective. The test must preserve enterprise routing signals, hold out complex workspaces, and be read on qualified revenue, 30/60-day retention, and pipeline quality, not signup volume. If qualified revenue does not move even as signups rise, that is a failure, not a partial success.

This addresses onboarding completion upstream and should carry into activation; if it does not, activation_messaging is the next slot, and it should be verified before use rather than trusted as summarized.
